subject: redPanda
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: red panda balancing on a mossy stone.
Style: Genshin Impact.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a full module for a red panda in Genshin Impact toon style, balancing on a mossy stone with the cel-shaded toolkit—working through the pose design with legs spread and tail extended for balance.

I'm figuring out the scale relationships between the panda and stone, placing the stone top at a specific height and positioning the hip joint accordingly, then deciding between a lathe-based boulder shape versus a flattened icosahedron with moss paint for the stone geometry.

Designing lathe profile for faceted stone shape...

I'll place the paw targets slightly sunk into the stone top, then work on dressing the stone with moss patches, mottled grey coloring, and a few grass blade cards around the edges for texture. Now I'm sketching the panda's skeleton coordinates, starting with hips and spine chain positioned relative to the stone top height.

Since red pandas have short legs with their belly close to the ground, I'm keeping the leg segments compact—around 0.075 each for upper and lower leg—so the hips sit higher while the paws reach down near the stone surface.

For the pose, I'll have the panda stand wide with all four legs planted and the tail arching up in an S-curve for balance, with ringed bands painted along it in rusty orange and darker stripes. For the skeleton structure, I'm planning joint hierarchy starting with a root hips joint, then building a spine chain through catmull-rom points up to the chest, figuring out how to name and resample the joints along that path.

Now I'm deciding the loft approach: the spine chain starts just behind the rump so it covers the whole body sweep, while the tail gets its own separate chain parented at the hips joint.

For coloring, I'm sketching a red panda coat palette with a toon cel-shading approach: a rusty-orange tone for the main coat and a dark brown/black tone for the belly, layering these with fur-edge treatments.

Now I'm thinking through the head shape: wide and round with cheek tufts, a dark short snout, white muzzle, white-rimmed round ears, and the characteristic tear-mark lines beneath the eyes.

I'm working out proportions so the big anime-style eyes sit above the muzzle without overlapping — placing eyes near the upper sides of the skull and keeping the muzzle centered lower down with a narrower width.

Now I'm working out the head bone placement relative to the neck and chest, positioning the skull center so it overlaps slightly with the chest radius without looking disjointed. I'm also laying out the body stations from rump to mid-body, tracking width, height, and vertical offset at each z-position to build a coherent skeletal profile.

Mapping out the spine chain as a catmull curve through the rump, hips, mid, chest, and shoulder stations, I'm deciding on naming the four spine segments and their role assignment for the rig.

Now I'm setting up the hips as root joint and working out the neck chain from the chest to the head, using a short two-point catmull spline with named joints for the neck base and tip, parented off the final spine joint.

Then I'm planning the head: a joint positioned near the top of the neck pointing forward, with a skull center and radii for shaping the panda's head sphere, plus a tapering neck tube that'll mostly be hidden by the ruff and head geometry.

Widening the skull radii for the characteristic broad red panda face, then working out cheek ruffs using zigzag-outline extrusions placed on either side of the face to mimic the fluffy white cheek fur.

I'll compute the tip point manually by cloning the hit vector and adding an offset, keeping the spike attached to the head bone. For ears, I'm planning large round triangular red panda ears with white-rimmed inner fur and orange outer surfaces, built from scaled half-sphere geometry.

Setting up a head coordinate helper for placing ear parts relative to the skull center, with dark outer ear coloring and a white inner tuft offset slightly forward.

Now I'm working out the facial features: a short white muzzle ellipsoid, a small dark nose at the front tip with a tiny highlight speck, and a separate lower jaw piece scaled smaller and positioned under the muzzle.

For the mouth, I'm skipping any inner tongue detail and keeping it closed, instead adding two short dark rods curving from center to each corner underneath the muzzle to suggest a simple smiling mouth line, attached to the jaw bone.

Now I'm thinking through the face markings for a red panda look—rusty tear stripes from eyes to mouth and white patches on cheeks and muzzle. I'll handle this with a procedural paint on the skull using local coordinates relative to the head center, defining conditions based on position to paint white cheek patches versus the base rusty-orange fur.

Still defining coloring logic...

Solving for the eye position using the ellipsoid geometry, I get x≈0.059, z≈0.0705. The tear lines sit slightly inward from there and taper down the cheek, staying clear of the white fur patches.

Now I'm checking the muzzle placement in front of the skull — looks fine at z≈0.075 with radius 0.05. Moving to the forelegs, I'm verifying the shoulder-to-foot reach distance against the limb segment lengths to confirm the IK solve is feasible (0.162 vs max reach 0.18), then working out the bend direction for the knee joint.

Attaching leg chains to spine joints now...

Setting leg radius from 0.045 to 0.034 with dark brown cel-shaded coloring. For the paw, I'm placing a flattened sphere at the foot's tip joint with a slight forward offset so it sinks naturally into the ground target position.

Adding small toe spheres at the paw front with tiny cream-colored claw cones, and binding them to the chain's tip joint since the three-bone chain guarantees a valid tip. Now moving on to building a thick, bushy, ringed tail starting from the rump position.

For the tail I'm plotting a curved path of points that sweeps backward and upward in an S-shape, totaling about 0.55 in length, with a radius profile that's thicker in the middle and tapers to a bushy tip. I'm planning alternating ring stripes of rust and darker rust along the tail's length using a banding pattern based on position.

Adding tail ring colors...

Using a tapered radius array for the tail sweep so it narrows toward the tip. I'm also considering adding scattered fur tuft cards on the tail and cheeks for texture, tinted with the paint color, though I'll keep the count moderate to manage complexity.

For the tint to work correctly on cards, I realize sampling paint by `s` won't work since cards don't carry a meaningful position parameter — instead I should project each card's point onto the tail's catmull path to find its closest `t` value and use that for the ring paint, which is more robust though potentially slower if computed per texel, so I may need to bake it ahead of time.

I'll skip cards on the tail and instead add a scalloped silhouette using a radius wobble function for fur texture, while placing cards on the head for cheek fur tinted grey-white using a tuft texture whose shading follows each part's color.

For the cheeks I'll scatter a cluster of tufts filtered to only hit the cheek region, colored cream-white, and consider similar fur accents for the forehead and ears while skipping the belly. I also want moss-covered stone geometry using cards in green tones, with the stone shape built from a lathe.

Now I'm defining the moss paint logic: blending height with noise to decide where moss appears, using light/dark moss tones with a cel-shaded edge transition, and falling back to a toon-shaded grey-violet stone color elsewhere. Writing moss paint function...

For the moss clumps I'm planning to scatter small flattened sphere shapes across the top of the stone, keeping them away from edges near the panda's paws, and varying their scale for a natural clustered look.

I'm also adding a few grass blade cards tinted in greens around the stone's rim, keeping things simple and skipping extras like mushrooms or flowers to avoid clutter, while considering a subtle glowing accent to tie in the anime cel-shaded aesthetic.

I'll keep the glow minimal, maybe just a handful of small pale glowing moss buds scattered on the stone as a nod to the Dendro style, then move on to refining the tail rings, head, and body details like the darker belly and legs.

For texture, I'm planning orange fur tuft cards scattered across the back where the surface normal faces upward, using a simple blade-shaped tuft texture plus a separate grass texture to give that Genshin-style coat detail while keeping shading tied to each card's frame normal.

For the body itself, I'm using the loft function on the spine stations to generate the main surface, with width running along the binormal and height along the normal as the path sweeps forward from rump to chest.

I want the loft stations to use the exact same catmull-rom points as the spine chain path so the bones and surface line up perfectly, resampling the chain by arc length into four segments.

For the neck I'll use three points with two spans giving two joints, and for the tail I'll use five points with five names including the tip, since the tail needs more articulation. Sweeping a chain across its full path should cover the whole surface, and the neck chain parents off the last spine joint, continuing its path from the spine's end position.

Now I'm defining the neck sweep radius tapering from 0.075 to 0.06, hidden inside the head and chest, colored with the coat's rust-and-dark pattern, then placing the head joint at the neck's endpoint and figuring out where to offset the skull center slightly forward of it.

Checking overlap between the chest front and head sphere back confirms they blend fine. I'm adjusting the head height upward slightly to sit level with the shoulder top for that alert, cute red panda posture, and considering head radii around 0.105/0.088/0.092 — a touch large for the chibi proportions but still working with the 0.2-wide body.

Now I'm setting up the eye decal targets against the skull surface, then defining the muzzle and nose parts with their own scaled positions relative to the head center.

I'm placing the nose highlight sphere and working out the jaw geometry—its joint position, scale, and bone orientation for the mouth structure.

Still calculating mouth geometry...

Actually, I'll skip the complex mouth lines and just rely on cel shading to suggest the jaw boundary. Next I'm adding thin white whisker rods fanning out from the muzzle sides, three per side, and positioning the ears as scaled spheres near the top of the skull.

For the ears, I'm orienting them to face mostly forward with a slight outward tilt, using dark brown-black for the outer shell and a smaller white ellipsoid offset inward for the inner ear detail, while leaving the tuft spikes as an optional detail to skip if it gets too fussy.

I'll add a dark rim visible behind the white front layer, then set up placement offsets for the ears along their directional axis. For paint, I'm using cream-white tones with a shadow gradient, and planning cheek fur tufts as small cone spikes positioned around the skull at various angles pointing outward and down.

For each spike, I'm computing the hit point and orienting it outward along the surface normal with a specific size and sides count, which should read as fluffy red panda cheeks when done.

Now I'm handling the rest of the coat—dark markings on the legs, a white chest and throat using the belly-facing normals, and scattering fur cards across the back with randomized size, bend, and lean so it reads as a soft coat texture, keeping triangle counts reasonable at this density.

I'm deciding to add ink outlines along the belly edge where the fur transitions, using a default ink color and width to give that cel-shaded line-art look, then setting up the normal-based threshold that separates the lighter coat color from the darker belly shading along the body's length.

For the legs I'm picking a dark brown tone to match real red panda coloring, then moving to the tail where I'm defining alternating ring colors based on position along its length, with a special tip color near the very end.

For the tail rings I'm deciding between orange and dark rust tones, maybe adding a pale cream accent, then settling on simple alternation with a darker tip. For the eyes I'm choosing an amber-brown iris to fit the stylized anime look while keeping the pink cheek blush for cuteness.

I'm also sorting out decal placement details — the eye projected onto the skull, mirroring settings for left versus right eye, and confirming rigid attachment to the head. I'm deciding to skip whiskers as an unnecessary extra, keeping the stone base simple without scattered pebbles, and letting the rig auto-attach parts to their nearest joints.

Now I'm working out the joint hierarchy: hips as the root joint, spine chain built from there with hind legs parenting off the hips and fore legs parenting off a later spine joint near the shoulder, checking that the z-coordinates along the spine arc line up so the shoulder position matches naturally.

I'm calculating limb geometry for the front and hind legs, computing root and target points for each and checking the resulting distances stay within reasonable bone-length limits before building the leg chains.

With all four limb lengths and bend directions set, I'm now sizing and positioning the paw ellipsoids at the foot targets and double-checking that the feet won't clip through the ground stone.

Checking clearance, I realize the hind feet reach too far back and would hang off the edge of the stone's top surface given its current radius, so I need to enlarge the stone or shift the panda's body forward to keep all four paws solidly planted.

I'm flattening the stone's top profile so the feet rest just above the surface rather than floating, adjusting the outline coordinates accordingly. To avoid the rock looking too uniform, I'm thinking about adding a couple of small secondary boulders off to the side for a more natural, asymmetric composition.

I'll simplify by skipping extra stones and instead use a faceted lathe with coarser segments for a crisp rock-like surface. For coloring, I'm varying moss coverage based on surface normal and noise so patches drip down the sides and cluster near the top, while filtering out clumps that would poke through near the paws.

Now I'm scattering small moss clumps along the stone's sloped edge, placing tiny glowing flowers on the moss border, and adding grass card scatter points across the upper stone surface.

Checking function signatures for scale arrays, decals, and card scattering against the kit examples to confirm the right parameter shapes before writing the actual calls.

I need to watch for unused imports since the typecheck seems strict about that. For the stone lathe shape, I'm thinking about bone attachment—since every mesh needs a bone and only one root joint is allowed, maybe the stone itself should be the root joint with hips as its child, so everything else rides along with it.

Settling on hips as root, with the stone bound to it so it moves naturally with the body. For the loft, I'm deciding the body path should bind to the spine chain alone, since hips mainly governs the hind legs and doesn't lie along the body curve.

Planning the tail as a swept curve along the tail chain with a tapering radius, using a rounded cap for a bushy tip, and adding moss paint details to the stone. Now I'm setting up the imports for the builder, toon shading kit, glow effect, and SVG utilities, making sure not to pull in anything unused like `mix`.

Defining color constants and stone position, then building out the fox palette—orange and rust tones for the lit coat, dark shadows, white highlights, a dark nose, and a gradient tail from orange through rust to a dark tip. I'm starting to configure the fur edge shader with teeth and ink outline parameters for the coat...

Now I'm designing SVG grass tuft and blade shapes as simple white/grey petal paths, then moving into moss color constants for painting texture onto the stone surface.

Writing stone paint logic...

Now I'm setting up the face paint function for the skull, defining coordinate offsets and a tear-line region based on vertical position.

Checking that the eye position overlaps the white edge zone correctly, and the eye's opaque almond shape covers any seam issues there. Moving on to coding the head parts...

Defining head coordinates and skull geometry...

Still working out the ear geometry...

I'll write my own normalization helper to avoid naming collisions, then set up the cheek tufts as spikes with four per side, skipping extra cards for simplicity. For whiskers, I'm defining rod elements running from the muzzle base to tip with a distinct flat cream color.

I'm skipping the forehead marking since the decal brow already covers that area, and now setting up the jaw joint and lower jaw sphere geometry for the head rig.

Jaw bone colored white, checking that the muzzle emerges cleanly below it without clipping. I'm placing the white muzzle sphere, nose shape, and a tiny glint sphere, making sure their positions align properly between the eyes.

Now I'm thinking through the neck sweep connecting to the skull, cheek ruff coloring, and adding fur tufts across the body with orange cel-shaded coloring driven by surface normals.

Skipping the spike-based tufts approach, I'll give the tail varying cross-section radii instead, scalloped from base to tip, with a path curving upward from the rump through a few S-shaped waypoints toward the tip.

The tail stays clear of the ground and stone, with lowest points resting correctly. Now I'm writing helper functions for vector creation and offsetting points along a direction by a given distance.

Defining leg positions...

Adding the paw sphere at the foot joint, checking that its vertical offset keeps it grounded against the leg sweep's end cap without floating or sinking too deep into the stone base.

I'm positioning three toe spheres splayed along the foot's front edge with small dark claw spikes angled forward, confirming they protrude just slightly past the paw front so they read visually without clipping oddly.

Now I'm setting up grass and moss scattering across the stone surface using a seeded RNG with minimum distance spacing, filtering placements by radial distance from the stone's center so growth stays within the rounded top area.

Still adding stems and flower geometry...

I'll skip the leaf emblem idea and instead scatter small colored flower cards across the moss for extra texture variety, then move on to defining the body loft stations with their positions, widths, and heights along the creature's form.

I'm checking the proportions—belly height, leg length, and overall body size—to make sure the red panda's stone base, torso, and ears add up correctly, around 0.65 total height including the stone section.

For the pose I'm keeping it neutral but raising the tail, and I'm defining the neck chain joints connecting from the spine's end point up through to the head, working out the right direction vectors and parent-joint relationships so the neck flows naturally into the head.

Now I'm setting all the head parts to share the same bone, then working out how to attach cheek tuft spikes using base and tip points so they angle outward and backward from the face, figuring out the right offsets and azimuth values for a natural-looking placement.

Adding small accent boulders near the base using faceted icosahedron shapes, darkening the stone color where it meets the ground for a weathered look.

Now I'm defining the grass tint colors and working out the face paint code and hit-filtering types for the callbacks.

Still refining shading details...
